blocks.text: Large language models achieve high scores on medical knowledge assessments, yet clinical reasoning requires actively deciding what to investigate under uncertainty. We developed an agentic evaluation framework in hematologic oncology in which models must proactively request clinical data across three sequential rounds before committing to a diagnosis and treatment plan. Across 32 frontier models, the best achieved only 68% overall accuracy. Information utilization - the fraction of available data actually requested - was the strongest predictor of diagnostic accuracy (R = 0.69, P < 0.001), yet utilization collapsed from 57% to 26% in the final round, leaving molecular and cytogenetic data critical for treatment selection unexamined. Reasoning traces scored high on a clinical reasoning rubric (91% above threshold) but decorrelated from accuracy, revealing a gap between locally coherent rationales and globally correct conclusions. Error analysis identified search satisficing, anchoring and premature closure as the dominant failure modes - the same cognitive biases that characterize novice clinicians under dual-process models of diagnostic reasoning. These findings demonstrate that the primary limitation of current models in clinical oncology is not insufficient medical knowledge but a systematic failure of information-seeking under uncertainty.

Clinical decision-making in hematologic oncology requires the sequential integration of incomplete and evolving information. Resource constraints and clinical urgency demand a stepwise, case-adapted approach in which each diagnostic step is selected based on its expected impact on the therapeutic decision at hand. Molecular profiling results arrive incrementally, treatment decisions must account for prior therapies and transplant history, and concurrent complications may fundamentally alter the therapeutic calculus. At each stage, clinicians must decide how to interpret partial results and when to act under uncertainty. This capacity to identify what information is needed and to prioritize appropriately constitutes a core competence of an experienced hematologist. In cognitive science, this process is formalized in dual-process models of diagnostic reasoning, where the transition from rapid pattern recognition to deliberate hypothesis testing depends critically on recognizing when initial impressions are insufficient.1 1

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on medical knowledge assessments and oncology decision support.2–4 Yet reliable active information-seeking by these systems remains insufficiently tested in subspecialty oncology.5–7 Multimodal AI systems that integrate information from radiology, histopathology, genomics, and clinical records8–11 and autonomous AI agents have demonstrated promising results in structured clinical tasks. However, all existing evaluations share a critical limitation: they present models with complete clinical information and assess the ability to interpret it, not the ability to decide what information to seek.12,13 Existing benchmarks present clinical information passively.14–16 In clinical practice, the direction of information flow is reversed: clinicians must actively decide what to investigate, interpret results as they arrive, and revise plans accordingly. This process of sequential planning under uncertainty separates clinical reasoning from medical knowledge retrieval. In human cognition, novice clinicians characteristically fail at exactly this juncture, exhibiting search satisficing, premature closure, and anchoring bias as described in Croskerry’s dual-process model. Whether large language models exhibit analogous information-seeking failures has not been systematically tested.17,18 Here we test this directly using OncoRounds, an agentic evaluation framework that requires proactive informationseeking in hematologic oncology. Models are presented with an initial clinical scenario and must actively request

clinical information, one item per turn, across three rounds of increasing complexity. This design separates the ability to identify relevant clinical data from the ability to interpret it, and evaluates both within a single, integrated framework. blocks.text: Alongside R-IDEA scoring, reasoning traces were annotated for cognitive biases and process errors using a taxonomy adapted from Croskerry's dual-process model of clinical reasoning.21 Errors were identified in 89 of 1,008 evaluations (8.8%), yielding 93 individual error annotations across the 17 models with full thinking traces (Table 4). Process errors were more frequent than cognitive biases. The most common error types were search satisficing, premature closure, and anchoring bias. Anchoring bias, the most frequent cognitive bias, appeared across multiple models, consistent with the diagnostic anchoring observed in the round-level trajectory analysis. Hallucinated information was rare, suggesting that models generally constrained their reasoning to the presented clinical data (Figure 3b). Error rates varied widely across models (Table 4). Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and GLM 5 had the lowest error rates (1.7% each), while Qwen3 Next 80B had the highest (26.7%). The majority of errors were of medium severity (56/93, 60.2%), followed by low (27/93, 29.0%) and high severity (10/93, 10.8%). In humanclinical reasoning, search satisficing, theprematureterminationof information search after identifying a plausible explanation, is a well-characterizedfailure mode.21 The present data suggest that LLMs exhibitananalogouspattern,likelycompoundedbytwoknownarchitecturalandbehaviorallimitations. First,LLMs exhibit positional attention biases that degrade retrieval of information positioned in the middle of long contexts,25 and performance on complex reasoning tasks deteriorates as context length increases, with models producing shorter and less reliable outputs.26 OncoRounds is demanding in this regard. By the final round, the accumulated interaction history of requests, released information items, prior diagnostic assessments, and reasoning traces can exceed 10,000 tokens per case, placing critical molecular data at exactly the context positions where retrieval is weakest. Second, Laban et al. demonstrated that LLMs perform significantly worse in multi-turn conversations than in equivalent single-turn instructions, with accuracy declining as interaction depth increases, compounded by premature assumptions from which models fail to recover.27 The round-over-round performance decline observed here is consistent with both phenomena, and the interaction between context saturation and multi-turn degradation may explain why the largest utilization drop occurs in the final round, where context is longest and the number of

Composite performance declined across rounds, with 25 of 32 models scoring lower in the final round than the first. This pattern does not indicate that additional data harms performance. Rather, later rounds demand progressively greater diagnostic precision as the reference standard shifts from syndromic identification to molecular subtyping per WHO classification, risk stratification, and treatment-refractory designations. Models consistently identified the correct disease category but failed to achieve the specificity required for actionable clinical classification, a pattern the trajectory analysis characterized as subtype refinement failure. Anchoring bias and premature closure, among the most frequently cited cognitive errors in clinical medicine,21 offer a partial mechanistic explanation. Recent work confirms that LLMs exhibit analogous vulnerabilities. Moëll et al. identified anchoring and difficulty integrating conflicting data as the most frequent errors in DeepSeek R1's medical reasoning,28 and Schmidgall et al. showed that cognitive biases reduce diagnostic accuracy across medical LLMs with varying resilience by model family.29 Ke et al. demonstrated that multi-agent frameworks with designated devil's advocate agents can partially mitigate such biases, improving accuracy from 0% to 76% in diagnostically challenging scenarios.30

blocks.text: The OncoRounds data extend these observations by showing that anchoring operates at a finer granularity than previously documented. Models did not anchor on incorrect disease categories but on an initial level of diagnostic resolution and failed to update toward the molecular precision that later-round evidence demanded. However, in hematologic oncology, where treatment selection depends directly on molecular subtype and risk classification, this level of detail is needed. Differential reasoning was the weakest scoring component for all 32 models, averaging 23 percentage points below diagnosticaccuracy. ThispatternwascorroboratedbytheR-IDEAevaluation,wherethealternativesdimensionwas among the lowest-scoring, and by the error taxonomy, where search satisficing and premature closure were the most frequent error types. However, differential diagnosis is also the most subjective component in the benchmark, as the clinical relevance and ranking of alternative diagnoses are less standardized than the primary diagnosis or treatment plan, making automated scoring less reliable for this category. With that caveat, the consistent deficit across all models and evaluation modalities suggests a genuine limitation rather than a scoring artifact. In hematologic oncology, the differential diagnosis determines which molecular and cytogenetic studies to pursue. A model that commits to AML without adequately considering ALL, or mixed-phenotype acute leukemia will fail to request the investigations needed to distinguish between them, compounding the information-gathering deficit observed above.

R-IDEA scores exceeded the high-quality threshold (6 of 10) in 91% of evaluations, yet mean accuracy remained 56.3%. This disconnect aligns with the faithfulness-plausibility gap described in recent reviews of medical LLM reasoning,31 whereby models produce well-structured reasoning traces that nonetheless arrive at incorrect conclusions. MedThink- Bench addressed this by evaluating step-by-step rationales against expert-authored references and achieved strong correlation with expert judgment (Pearson r = 0.87), but within a static format where all relevant information is provided upfront.32 OncoRounds adds a temporal dimension. Even when reasoning quality within a single solve attempt is high, the cumulative effect of inadequate information gathering together with the context-length limitations discussed above can undermine the final diagnosis. Across 32 frontier large language models evaluated in complex hematologic oncology, the primary performancelimiting factor was not medical knowledge but a systematic failure to seek the clinical information on which treatment decisions depend. Information utilization was the strongest predictor of accuracy, yet models exhibited searchsatisficing,anchoringandprematureclosure-thesamefailuremodesdocumentedinnovicehumanclinicians under dual-process models of diagnostic reasoning. The convergence of these failure patterns across fundamentally different cognitive architectures suggests that information-seeking under uncertainty represents a general challenge for systems trained primarily on complete-case presentations. Addressing this limitation will require training paradigms that explicitly model active information gathering and iterative hypothesis testing, moving beyond the passive interpretation tasks on which current systems excel. 6

OncoRoundsisaninteractive,turn-basedbenchmarkforevaluatingLLMclinicalreasoninginhematologiconcology. The benchmark simulates clinical decision-making through three progressive rounds of information disclosure. Round 1 (outpatient presentation) provides vital signs, chief complaint, and point-of-care diagnostics. Round 2 (inpatient workup) adds imaging, biopsies, and specialized consultations. Round 3 (definitive characterization) includes full pathology, cytogenetics, and molecular markers. A detailed treatment history, including prior lines of therapy and refractoriness status, was withheld until Round 3 to prevent premature unblinding of disease subtypes in earlier rounds. At each turn, models choose between requesting a single additional piece of clinical information or committing to a diagnostic and treatment solution. This single-request-per-turn constraint enforces clinical prioritization, requiring models to reason about which information would be most valuable given what is already known. The benchmark architecture is depicted in Figure 4. Thirty-two models (Supplementary Table 1) were evaluated across 20 cases (Table 1), each progressing through all three clinical rounds.

Twenty clinical cases were developed spanning the spectrum of hematologic malignancies. Each case comprises a patient profile (demographics, chief complaint, vital signs), round-specific clinical settings describing the available diagnostic capabilities, a set of information items gated by round availability, and a reference standard for each round. Reference standards consist of a working diagnosis, differential diagnoses, and a treatment plan in which each action is annotated with its intention (therapeutic, diagnostic, or supportive) and priority level (1 through 3). Information items represent clinical data obtainable in each round's setting: complete blood counts, coagulation studies, and bedside imaging in the outpatient round; tissue biopsies, immunophenotyping, and focused imaging during inpatient workup; and molecular panels, cytogenetics, and measurable residual disease assessments in the definitive phase. Cases were developed de novo by a board-certified hematologist (KB) with 10 years of experience, rather than adapted from published case reports or public repositories, to minimize the risk of data leakage into model training corpora. The parser received the candidate's free-text request together with the list of available information items and their round-availability constraints, and returned a structured mapping indicating whether the request was valid and which item, if any, it corresponded to. Solution attempts were evaluated by a judge ensemble of five parallel GPT-5 Mini instances. Each judge independently compared the candidate's working diagnosis, differential diagnoses, and treatment plan against the 7

round-specific reference standard, assigning one of three labels to each element: correct (clinically accurate and complete), partially correct (directionally correct but incomplete or imprecise), or incorrect. For the working diagnosis, the correct label required an exact match or accepted synonym; partially correct was assigned for the correct disease family with a missing critical modifier. Each candidate differential diagnosis was independently labeled against the reference set, regardless of how many the model proposed. Treatment plan items were scored across three sub-dimensions: action (whether the intervention matched the reference), intention (therapeutic, diagnostic, or supportive), and priority (scored correct if matching, partially correct if off by one level, incorrect if off by two or more). Final labels were determined by majority vote across the five judges. When no label achieved a strict majority, partially correct was selected as the tiebreaker, reflecting a conservative approach to borderline assessments. Thejudgeensemblewascalibratedagainstindependentscoringbyaboard-certifiedhematologist(KB) across all 20 cases (1,007 paired evaluation items spanning all three clinical rounds) to verify alignment on labeling criteria and partial-credit boundaries. Because the three scoring labels (correct, partially correct, incorrect) form an ordered scale on which a two-category disagreement carries greater clinical consequence than a one-category disagreement,quadraticweightedCohen's 𝜅 wasusedtoassessinter-rateragreement,yieldingsubstantialagreement

(𝜅 = 0.804). The AI judge was systematically stricter than the human expert, with 10.7% of ratings being AI-stricter versus 7.1% expert-stricter. The most frequent source of disagreement was the AI downgrading expert partially correct ratings to incorrect (48 items).

Overall performance was quantified as balanced accuracy, defined as the unweighted mean of three category-level accuracies: diagnosis, differential diagnosis, and treatment. Labels were converted to numeric scores of 1.0 (correct), 0.5 (partially correct), and 0.0 (incorrect), and category accuracy was computed as the ratio of earned points to maximum possible points, expressed as a percentage. For differential diagnoses, a greedy best-N matching strategy was applied: all candidate labels were sorted by quality (correct first, then partially correct, then incorrect) and only the top N were counted toward the score, where N equaled the number of reference differentials. A model proposing 10 differentials against five references would thus have its five best-matching labels scored. To discourage list-padding, a penalty of one point was subtracted for each candidate differential beyond a threshold of max(10, 2N), with the total floored at zero. Treatment was scored identically using the same best-N selection and anti-gaming penalty applied to the three sub-dimensions (action, intention, priority) jointly, yielding a maximum of three points per reference treatment item. Clinical reasoning quality was assessed using an adapted version of the Revised-IDEA (R-IDEA) rubric.20 The rubric evaluates four dimensions: Interpretive Summary (I; 0 to 4 points), reflecting synthesis of clinical data into a coherent narrative; Differential Diagnosis (D; 0 to 2), assessing breadth and prioritization of diagnostic hypotheses; Explanation (E; 0 to 2), capturing mechanistic reasoning linking findings to diagnoses; and Alternatives (A; 0 to 2), evaluating consideration of competing hypotheses and disconfirming evidence. Dimension scores sum to a composite total ranging from 0 to 10, with six or above considered high-quality reasoning. This analysis was restricted to the 17 models that produced full thinking traces, yielding 1,008 model-case-round entries. Evaluator agents (Claude Opus 4.6) independently scored each thinking trace given the clinical scenario and scoring. A random sample of 50 entries was independently reviewed by the authors (KKB) to verify agent scoring. Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for mean R-IDEA scores were computed using 10,000 replicates with the percentile method.

Reasoning errors were annotated using a taxonomy adapted from Croskerry's dual-process model of clinical reasoning.21 The taxonomy distinguished cognitive biases from process errors. Cognitive biases comprised anchoring bias (fixating on an initial impression despite contradictory information), confirmation bias (selectively attendingtosupportiveevidence),prematureclosure(acceptingadiagnosisbeforeadequateverification),availability bias(overweightingeasilyrecalleddiagnoses), andsearchsatisficing(terminatingthediagnosticsearchafterfinding one plausible explanation). Process errors comprised hallucinated information (incorporating findings not present 8

in the case data), logical contradiction (making mutually incompatible claims), and over-differentiating (generating excessively broad differential lists without stratification). Three error types captured by the benchmark's existing scoring mechanism and information-gathering analysis were excluded: incomplete workup, missed key findings, and incorrect diagnosis. Each error was graded on a four-level severity scale (low, medium, high, critical) based on potential clinical impact, and was judged against the information available to the model at the time of the error rather than retrospectively against the complete case. Error annotations were produced by the same evaluator agents (Claude Opus 4.6) used for R-IDEA scoring, applied simultaneously during trace evaluation.

Information-gathering strategy was characterized by two metrics computed per model-case-round entry. Request precision was defined as the proportion of valid requests (those successfully matched to an available information item and released to the model) out of total requests made. Information utilization was defined as the proportion of available information items in a given round that were actually requested by the model.

Diagnostic trajectories tracked changes in working diagnosis accuracy from the first to the final clinical round. Model-case pairs with valid diagnosis labels across all three rounds were classified into four mutually exclusive categories: sustained correct (correct at both R1 and R3), recovered (incorrect at R1 but correct at R3), deteriorated (correctatR1butincorrectatR3),andsustainedincorrect(incorrectatbothR1andR3). Partiallycorrectdiagnoses were grouped with incorrect for trajectory classification.

Pearson correlations with one-sided tests assessed associations between model-level information-gathering metrics (request precision and information utilization). R-IDEA scores and overall benchmark accuracy. Kruskal-Wallis tests evaluated differences in number of requests across clinical rounds. Pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons were used for post-hoc group comparisons of R-IDEA scores and error rates. The maximum sample space comprised 1,920 model-case-round entries (32 models by 20 cases by three rounds), of which 1,896 were completed (634 in R1, 631 each in R2 and R3). R-IDEA evaluation encompassed 1,008 entries across the 17 models with full thinking traces. Diagnostic trajectory analysis included
complete model-case triads. A p value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

This supplementary appendix presents 49 curated reasoning trace excerpts from 17 large language models, programmatically selected from 1,066 R-IDEA evaluation entries. Each excerpt includes the clinical context, the evaluator’s assessment, and a verbatim passage from the model’s internal reasoning trace. Excerpts are organized into three sections: •Error Type Taxonomy (26 excerpts), illustrating all 7 cognitive error types identified during evaluation • R-IDEADimensionAnalysis(16excerpts),contrastinglowandhighperformanceoneachofthefourR-IDEA dimensions • Exemplary Reasoning (7 excerpts), showcasing high-fidelity clinical reasoning (total R-IDEA≥9, no errors) Selection methodology.Excerpt selection and annotation were performed with the assistance of Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic). A Python script scored candidates by evaluator quote availability, error severity, explanation quality, and model diversity, then extracted verbatim passages from the corresponding thinking trace files. For error type excerpts, candidates were scored by evaluator quote availability, error severity, explanation quality, and model diversity. For R-IDEA dimensions, the two lowest- and highest-scoring entries per dimension were selected with family-level diversity constraints. Exemplary excerpts required perfect or near-perfect scores (total≥ 9) with no identifiederrors,diversifiedacrosscasesandmodelfamilies. Allexcerptswerereviewedbytheauthorsforaccuracy and representativeness.

Severity: high Evaluator:Failed to update diagnosis despite additional pathologic data being available. Continued to anchor on PTLD without considering BPDCN, which is the hardest case across all models in this benchmark. The differential did not include any plasmacytoid dendritic cell entities. Error detail:Despite moving to R2 with biopsy/flow cytometry capabilities, the model maintained PTLD without incorporating new pathologic data that would distinguish BPDCN from PTLD. BPDCN has distinctive markers (CD4+, CD56+, CD123+, BDCA-2+) that differ from typical PTLD. Thinking trace (step 8): [...] So the user should request bone marrow biopsy. Alternatively, the skin biopsy has already been requested in the previous solve, but maybe the user needs to confirm with a specific request for it. Wait, but in the previous solve, the user included skin biopsy as part of the solution. But according to the problem instructions, you must request information one piece at a time until you are confident. However, when solving, you provide the treatment plan. But in the current round 2, the patient is now inpatient, so perhaps the user can proceed to solve with the necessary tests. But the previous solve was evaluated as partially correct, so maybe the working diagnosis is correct but differentials or treatment plan incorrect. Looking at the evaluation: working_diagnosis was partially_correct. The differentials had one correct and others incorrect. For the treatment plan, first item correct, second priority partially correct, others incorrect.
